commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Benchmark] Don't count content-free chunks as streamed outputs in chat
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

The chat benchmark clients count the opening role-only chunk as a streamed output, so TTFT is measured to a chunk with no output in it and the first real token appends a spurious ITL sample. A check prevented this between #3768 and #12288; this restores it in a form that also handles `reasoning` and `tool_calls`. Original report: #3759.

Benchmark client only. No engine, scheduler or serving code is touched, and no measured figure here reflects a change in how fast vLLM runs.

## Claims

- TTFT for `--backend openai-chat` is measured to the opening `delta: {"role": "assistant", "content": ""}` chunk, which carries no output.
- As a result 208 of 600 requests recorded `len(itl) == output_tokens`, which cannot happen when every interval sits between two tokens; there are at most `output_tokens - 1`. `/v1/completions` on the same server recorded exactly 200 x 255 samples and zero impossible counts.
- Every request on `main` carried a first ITL sample timing the role chunk, median 4 microseconds, so the minimum and low percentiles time metadata arrival. The error runs in the flattering direction: `main` reports chat as slightly faster than it is. With the fix, the minimum and each request's first sample rise to real decode intervals, and vLLM's actual speed is unchanged.
- This does **not** materially change any printed summary metric. Mean and median TTFT, ITL and TPOT all move by less than the run-to-run spread. The fix is to the sample array, which `--save-detailed` writes to JSON.
- 43 lines across the two clients, no new abstraction, no change to `async_request_openai_completions` or `async_request_openai_audio`.

## Validation

Four behaviours added to `tests/benchmarks/test_endpoint_request_func_timing.py`, parametrized over the packaged and legacy clients. 18 tests to 26, all passing. All eight fail against current `main`:

| behaviour | fails on `main` as |
|---|---|
| opening role chunk is not a streamed output | `assert 5 == (5 - 1)` on the interval count |
| mid-stream content-free chunk adds no interval | `assert 4 == (3 - 1)` |
| stream with no streamed output is rejected | `assert not output.success`; `main` marks it successful |
| token rendering as an empty string is counted | `assert len(output.itl) == 2`, got 3, TTFT on the role chunk |

```
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/benchmarks/test_endpoint_request_func_timing.py -v
```

`pre-commit run --files` clean on all three files. The test file gains 188 lines and loses 2: two small chunk builders, `_role_chunk` and `_empty_chunk`, the four tests, and the module docstring reworded to describe them. The two removed lines are the old docstring wording. No existing test function is modified and no other test file is touched.

End-to-end on one RTX 3080, `Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B`, three interleaved blocks per side against a single server, 200 requests each, 600 per side, 256 output tokens, concurrency 64:

```
vllm bench serve --model Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B --port 8031 --backend openai-chat \
  --endpoint /v1/chat/completions --dataset-name random --num-prompts 200 \
  --output-len 256 --max-concurrency 64 --save-result --save-detailed
```

Across those 600 requests on `main`:

- all 600 had a first sample under 0.1 ms, timing the arrival of the role chunk, median 0.0040 ms. That is exactly one spurious sample per request and never more than one, and it is what drags the reported minimum ITL down to 0.0025 ms.
- 208 recorded `len(itl) == output_tokens`, more intervals than exist between that many tokens. These are the requests where no two tokens happened to share a read, so nothing offset the extra sample. The other 392 carried it too and landed under the limit.

On this branch, no request records `len(itl) == output_tokens` and none exceeds `output_tokens - 1`. Two of 600 had a first sample under 0.1 ms, both from two tokens arriving in a single read.

Total sample counts are not compared here. They differ between separate runs against a live server because the server coalesces tokens differently each time, so a gap between two runs' totals is not evidence of anything.

`/v1/completions` on the same server, same workload, recorded exactly 51,000 samples for 200 requests of 256 tokens, which is 200 x 255, and no impossible counts.

<details>
<summary>Printed summary metrics, which do not meaningfully change</summary>

Pooled over the three blocks per side, with the spread across `main`'s own three blocks for comparison:

| metric | main | this branch | delta | main's block spread |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mean TTFT | 463.74 ms | 251.13 ms | -212.61 | 724.23 |
| Median TTFT | 332.08 ms | 232.07 ms | -100.01 | 442.91 |
| P99 TTFT | 2465.88 ms | 423.67 ms | -2042.21 | 2293.71 |
| Mean ITL | 8.99 ms | 6.11 ms | -2.88 | 8.71 |
| Median ITL | 4.81 ms | 4.73 ms | -0.07 | 0.08 |
| P99 ITL | 114.96 ms | 53.65 ms | -61.32 | 71.91 |
| Mean TPOT | 8.94 ms | 5.98 ms | -2.96 | 8.79 |

Every delta is smaller than the spread between `main`'s own blocks, so none of it is a real difference; the pooled TTFT gap is mostly `main`'s first block being a cold start. The role chunk and the first token arrive about 4 microseconds apart, against swings of 85 ms in Mean TTFT between `main`'s two warm blocks alone.

The GPU also drives a display and was not idle during these runs. That is why the comparison is interleaved and why the spread column is included.

</details>

## Details

### Root cause

#3759 reported a chat TTFT of 0.005 s and printed the chunk it had been measured to, a role-only delta with `content: null`. @ywang96 identified the role chunk as the cause and #3768 added:

```python
delta = data["choices"][0]["delta"]
if delta.get("content", None):
```

#12288 restructured the same block to read token counts from the usage chunk. That required tolerating a trailing chunk with `choices: []`, since `data["choices"][0]` raises on it, and the gate became:

```python
if choices := data.get("choices"):
    content = choices[0]["delta"].get("content")
```

`content` is still read but no longer decides anything. The packaged client in `vllm/benchmarks/lib/` has the same shape. #3768's own note explains why nothing caught it: "This does not affect existing CI results since by default vLLM uses completions instead of chat completions for benchmarking."

### Tokens that render as empty strings

#12288 left this note on the completions side:

```python
if choices := data.get("choices"):
    # Note that text could be empty here
    # e.g. for special tokens
    text = choices[0].get("text")
```

That is correct: a token can decode to an empty string under `skip_special_tokens=True`, and dropping it would lose a real interval. #3768's truthiness gate would drop it. So the check here tests whether the chunk carries a token:

```python
if delta.get("content") or delta.get("reasoning") or delta.get("tool_calls") or delta.get("function_call"):
    return True
return delta.get("content") == "" and "role" not in delta
```

The two cases are distinguishable on the wire. An empty-rendering token serialises as `{"content": ""}`. The opening chunk serialises as `{"role": "assistant", "content": ""}`, and `role` is set only there, on the first iteration of `chat_completion_stream_generator`, and on no other `DeltaMessage` in the streaming path. A suppressed or finish chunk serialises as `{}`. A third-party server that repeats `role` on every chunk is unaffected, because a chunk with real content satisfies the first condition.

Three of the four fields, `content`, `reasoning` and `tool_calls`, are what vLLM's own streaming logger checks to decide whether a delta carried anything, in the same file. `function_call` is the fourth and vLLM never emits it; it is there because OpenAI's legacy spec puts it on streaming deltas and these clients are pointed at third-party OpenAI-compatible servers too.

### Tradeoffs and notes

The gate is a named helper with one call site per file, which §3.3 of the PR checklist would normally have inlined. It is kept because the two clients must stay in sync, per #55508, and a shared name makes a divergence between them visible; and because the second condition needs the comment explaining why an empty string counts, which reads badly inline.

Content-free chunks now reach the `elif usage:` branch, which the `if choices:` arm used to swallow. Under `continuous_usage_stats` the opening chunk carries both `choices` and `usage`, so its `completion_tokens: 0` is read and then overwritten by every later chunk. For servers that attach usage to an empty finish chunk with no trailing `choices: []` chunk, the count is now captured where it was dropped before.

`most_recent_timestamp` advances only inside the gated branch, so #55508's `latency - ttft == sum(itl)` guarantee is unchanged. #54708's rejection of tokenless streams is unchanged and now also fires on a stream whose chunks all carry content-free `choices`.

### Relation to #46652

#46652 proposed inserting zero-duration ITL samples so `len(itl)` matched the token count. `docs/benchmarking/cli.md` says ITL records only the gaps between streamed outputs and adds no zero-duration gaps for tokens in the same output, so #46652 is closed. This PR removes a sample with no output on either side of it. Both came out of #27485, which the stale bot closed; the reasoning and tool-parser case reported there is a different cause.

### Duplicate check

Nobody is fixing this. Every reference to #3759, #3768 and #12288 across issues and PRs is a coincidental numeric match; the 190 hits for 12288 are hidden and intermediate sizes. The regression was never re-reported after #12288 merged, so #3759 is still the only issue describing it.

A search by fix shape found nothing either. No PR restores a content gate, and `_choice_has_streamed_output` has no hits. #55508 touched this exact function on 2026-09-13 to make TTFT and latency accounting consistent across endpoints and left the gate ungated. #28183 attempted per-token ITL from continuous usage stats and was closed unmerged without adding a gate.

Open PRs touching either client file are #49720, #51155, #51172, #55719, #57519 and #58734. None modify the chunk gating. My own #46652 is in this area and is being closed.

#59722 is related. It reports the Rust `vllm-bench` chat backend counting token-less streams as successful and notes that Python fails them, which is true for the case tested there: a stream with no `choices` chunks at all, which `first_chunk_received` already rejects. It is not true for a stream whose chunks all carry content-free `choices`, which is the third behaviour above.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix] Reject LoRA at config time for models without SupportsLoRA
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Reject `enable_lora=True` during config validation for models that don't implement `SupportsLoRA`, instead of failing later inside EngineCore. Fixes #61850.

## Claims

- `LLM(model="Zyphra/Zamba2-7B-instruct", enable_lora=True)` now fails during config validation (a `ValidationError` from `VllmConfig`) with `LoRA is not supported for Zamba2ForCausalLM (Zyphra/Zamba2-7B-instruct). ...` instead of a bare `AssertionError` in EngineCore surfacing as `RuntimeError: Engine core initialization failed`.
- The check applies to every registered model without `SupportsLoRA` (125 architectures today), not only Zamba2 and Mamba2.
- No behavior change for models that support LoRA, or for any model run without `enable_lora`.

## Validation

Reproducer: the snippet from #61850, run on the CPU backend with `load_format="dummy"` (the failure happens in the model constructor, before weights load).

| Model | `enable_lora` | Before (main @ a97d19d792) | After |
|---|---|---|---|
| Zyphra/Zamba2-7B-instruct | True | `AssertionError` at `zamba2.py:719` → `Engine core initialization failed` | `ValidationError` at config validation, no EngineCore started |
| Zyphra/Zamba2-1.2B-instruct | False | starts and generates | starts and generates |
| yujiepan/mamba2-codestral-v0.1-tiny-random | True | `AssertionError` at `mamba2.py:106` → `Engine core initialization failed` | `ValidationError` at config validation |
| yujiepan/mamba2-codestral-v0.1-tiny-random | False | starts and generates | starts and generates |
| Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B | True | starts and generates | starts and generates |

<details>
<summary>Reproducer</summary>

```python
import sys
from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams

if __name__ == "__main__":
    model, lora = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2] == "lora"
    llm = LLM(model=model, enable_lora=lora, max_model_len=512, seed=42, load_format="dummy")
    print(llm.generate(["The capital of France is"], SamplingParams(temperature=0.0, max_tokens=8)))
```

</details>

Tests:

```bash
pytest tests/models/test_registry.py tests/test_config.py
```

- New tests: `test_registry_supports_lora` and `test_lora_rejected_at_config_time_for_unsupported_model`. They pass with this change; with the source changes reverted, the four cases that check the new behavior fail.
- Full `tests/models/test_registry.py` and `tests/test_config.py`: 838 passed vs. 833 on main, no new failures. The 14 failures that occur on both branches come from gated `meta-llama` checkpoints and CPU-environment limits.
- `ruff check` and `ruff format` pass.

Validated on the CPU backend only. The change touches config validation and the model registry, not device code; both test files run in CI (`models_basic.yaml`, `engine.yaml`).

## Details

**Root cause:** whether a model supports LoRA is already known from the `SupportsLoRA` interface, but it was only checked in `LoRAModelRunnerMixin.load_lora_model` (`lora_model_runner_mixin.py:47`), after the model is constructed inside the worker. `Zamba2Model` and `Mamba2Model` guard against LoRA with a bare `assert` in their constructors, which runs first, so the existing descriptive error was never reached, and the failure was only visible in EngineCore's stderr.

**Fix:** follows the existing pattern used for pipeline parallelism (`supports_pp` → `ModelConfig.is_pp_supported` → checked in `ModelConfig.verify_with_parallel_config`):

- `registry.py`: record `supports_lora` in `_ModelInfo`, computed with the existing `supports_lora()` helper.
- `config/model.py`: expose it as `ModelConfig.is_lora_supported`.
- `config/lora.py`: raise in `LoRAConfig.verify_with_model_config`, which already runs during `VllmConfig` validation.
- `zamba2.py`, `mamba2.py`: drop the now-unreachable asserts.

**Notes for reviewers:**

- No configuration that worked before is newly rejected: the runtime check calls the same `supports_lora()` on an instance of the same class, and no model sets `supports_lora` dynamically. Across all 390 loadable architectures, the class-level check also logs none of `supports_lora()`'s attribute-mismatch warnings.
- Cached model info from older versions lacks the new field; `_ModelInfo(**cached)` then raises, which `_load_modelinfo_from_cache` already catches, so the model is re-inspected.
- The runtime check in `LoRAModelRunnerMixin` is left in place.
- #61870 replaces the two asserts with `ValueError` in the constructors. That gives a clearer message, but it still runs inside EngineCore, so the user-facing error remains `Engine core initialization failed` (checked with the same reproducer). This PR moves the check to config validation, as the issue requests.

commits.pr_title: [Multimodal][Docs] State that retried media downloads count toward the request budget
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

Make it visible that `VLLM_MAX_MEDIA_REQUEST_DOWNLOAD_SIZE_MB` counts retried download attempts. As discussed above with @jperezdealgaba and @DarkLight1337, counting them is intentional: it stops a media URL that keeps disconnecting from transferring several times the limit through retries. This PR keeps that behavior and says so in the error message and in `docs/usage/security.md`.

## Claims

- The budget error now reads `Request media downloads exceed VLLM_MAX_MEDIA_REQUEST_DOWNLOAD_SIZE_MB=… (N bytes received, including retried attempts).`, so an operator seeing it for media under the limit knows why.
- The `security.md` row now says the budget includes "concurrent downloads and retried attempts".
- New sync and async tests pin the restrictive behavior: a fetch that fails mid-body and is retried is charged for both attempts and raises with that message.
- No behavior change.

## Validation

```
$ pytest tests/test_connections.py
main:    2 failed, 7 passed  (new tests: message lacks "including retried attempts")
this PR: 9 passed
```

`pytest tests/test_connections.py tests/test_audio_media_size_precheck.py tests/multimodal/media -m "skip_global_cleanup or cpu_test"`: 110 passed, 3 failed. The 3 failures also happen on `main` in my environment: PyAV isn't installed.

`pre-commit run --hook-stage manual` on the changed files: all hooks pass (ruff, typos, markdownlint, mypy, test tethering, SPDX).

## Details

This PR originally refunded a failed attempt's bytes before the retry. That was rejected for the security reason above (see @jperezdealgaba's comment and the earlier thread on #61226), and the scope was changed to documenting the behavior, per @DarkLight1337. The branch history shows both commits; the final diff is one line in `vllm/connections.py`, one line in `docs/usage/security.md`, and tests.

The test helpers in `tests/test_connections.py` now accept an exception in the chunk list, to simulate a connection dropping mid-body.

**Duplicate check:** searched open/closed issues and PRs for `MediaRequestDownloadBudget` and `VLLM_MAX_MEDIA_REQUEST_DOWNLOAD_SIZE_MB`; nothing else changes this message or doc row.

**AI assistance:** Claude (Anthropic) helped write this change. I reviewed every changed line and ran the tests above myself.

commits.pr_title: [ROCm][Perf][DSv4.1] Mono decode for the DSpark draft layers
commits.pr_body:
<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

DSv4.1-Flash mono decode (MI355X, `--monokernel`): the DSpark draft's three layers now run on the mono K1 / K2 kernels too, as ATOM's `DraftMonoRunner` does, instead of vLLM's per-op path. Follow-up to #60397 and #61082; they follow `--monokernel` like the target's layers, with no new switch. Overlaps files with #60731 (gfx942 port), so whichever merges second needs a rebase.

## Claims

- The draft's three layers cost about 227 us of kernel time per step on mono, in place of about 640 us on the original path (graph profile, TP4 c1): about 414 us less GPU time a step.
- AgentX at c1, per-request ITL p50 is 0.030 ms (1.8%) lower than InferenceX's run with `--monokernel`, at TP4 (1.646 against 1.678 ms) and at TP2 (1.970 against 2.000 ms).
- Draft quality is unchanged: DSpark mean acceptance length 3.889 / 3.935 (TP4) and 3.917 (TP2) against 3.899 / 3.896 without, and GSM8K 0.975 / 0.972.
- Target layers' kernels are untouched: their ISA is identical to `main`'s.

## Validation

All on MI355X, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, the InferenceX #3690 recipe, `main` at `ce49c47cbb` plus this PR unless a row says otherwise. "Off" is the same build with the draft layers on vLLM's path (a throwaway env switch for the A/B, not in this PR).

**Layer level.** The draft layers against the original layers on real eager decode steps (TP4 c1 and TP2 c1, 5- and 10-row steps), same inputs: x output cosine >= 0.99975 (relative L2 up to 2.3%, the MoE's top-3 routing near-ties), residual, post / comb / pre mixes >= 0.9999 cosine.

**Acceptance and accuracy** (real block rejection, GSM8K as in InferenceX's DSv4.1-Flash eval: custom `gsm8k` task, chat, 5-shot multiturn, `max_tokens` 12288, 64 requests in flight, full 1,319):

| | draft on mono: GSM8K strict / flexible; mean acceptance length | draft off |
|---|---|---|
| TP4 | 0.9750 / 0.9742; 3.889 (3.935 on the final rebase) | 0.9750 / 0.9742; 3.899 |
| TP2 | 0.9719 / 0.9712; 3.917 | 0.9727 / 0.9719; 3.896 |

**AgentX, c1, 3,600 s** (InferenceX's `infx.bench agentic` client, the #3690 recipe with `--monokernel`, DSpark with synthetic acceptance 3.51, the Rust frontend). Reference: InferenceX's run [38377181342](https://github.com/SemiAnalysisAI/InferenceX/actions/runs/38377181342) (same recipe, nightly 5555a2d8, its own node). TP4 and TP2 ran at the same time on one node. The confidence intervals are bootstrap over the per-request ITL of the profiling phase (about 330 requests an arm).

| | TP4 PR | TP4 ref | TP2 PR | TP2 ref |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ITL p50 (ms), from the summary | 1.650 | 1.680 | 1.970 | 2.000 |
| per-request ITL p50 (ms), diff [95% CI] | 1.646 | 1.678: -0.032 [-0.034, -0.027] | 1.970 | 2.000: -0.030 [-0.034, -0.026] |
| per-request ITL p90 (ms), diff [95% CI] | 1.690 | 1.757: -0.068 [-0.189, +0.012] | 2.053 | 2.178: -0.125 [-0.292, +0.196] |
| interactivity p50 / p90 (tok/s/user) | 607.6 / 591.8 | 596.1 / 569.1 | 507.6 / 487.1 | 499.9 / 459.1 |
| TTFT p50 / p90 (s) | 0.170 / 0.247 | 0.245 / 0.336 | 0.183 / 0.293 | 0.210 / 0.383 |
| E2E p50 (s) | 1.85 | 1.93 | 2.14 | 2.18 |
| requests completed | 335 | 331 | 318 | 316 |

The p50 gain is outside the noise at both TP sizes; the p90 interactivity gain (+4.0% and +6.1%) is not (its interval spans zero), and the TTFT difference is the node, not this PR (prefill is untouched). The reference is not a same-node baseline, so the p50 difference also includes any difference of node, image and commit; an earlier run on the same node of `main` plus only #61934's change (a different kernel change) gave ITL p50 1.670 / 2.000 ms (per-request 1.675 / 1.998).

**Kernel time** (graph-mode torch profile, TP4 c1, draft on mono): K1 about 20 us and K2 about 56 us a layer for the three draft layers (227 us a step); the non-target kernels of a step total 1.76 ms against 2.17 ms with the draft off (excluding all-reduce spin-waits).

**Tests.** `tests/models/test_dsv41_mono_decode.py`: 41 pass, 3 new (the draft layer takes the mono path on its own runner, its first layer takes the broadcast embedding, a layer takes only its own SWA row width). The K1 / K2 ISA of the target builds at TP4, M=6 is identical to `main`'s (`FLYDSL_DUMP_IR` diff: 0 lines).

**Accuracy** (RFC #59665 protocol, as in #60397: thinking on, `reasoning_effort` high, temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, 8 requests in flight a server, DSpark with block rejection, `--monokernel` so the draft layers run on mono; pass@1, ± is the standard error across questions). The baselines are #60397's numbers; no reference arm of this build was rerun.

| | this PR | #60397 |
|---|---|---|
| TP2 GPQA-Diamond (8 samples a question) | 84.8 ± 2.2 | 85.3 ± 2.2 reference, 85.1 ± 2.2 mono |
| TP2 AIME25 (16 samples a problem) | 98.3 ± 0.9 | 99.4 ± 0.3 reference, 98.3 ± 0.8 mono |
| TP4 GPQA-Diamond (4 samples a question) | 84.5 ± 2.3 | 85.2 ± 2.2 mono |
| TP4 AIME25 (8 samples a problem) | 98.8 ± 0.7 | 100.0 mono (240/240) |

AIME25's wrong samples: 8 of 480 at TP2 (3 empty, out of the 64K budget; 4 on one hard problem) and 3 of 240 at TP4 (1 empty).

**RULER NIAH** (lm-eval, prefix-free chat copies, thinking on, greedy, 40 samples a cell): `niah_single_1`, `niah_multikey_2` and `niah_multikey_3` at 32K, 128K and 256K score 40/40 in every cell at both TP2 and TP4, as in #60397.

## Details

The draft layers are `DeepseekV4DecoderLayer`s with window-only attention (compress ratio 0, no indexer), so the kernels need no new stage. What differs is carried by the build and the step's integers:

- **Routing:** 128 routed experts, top-3 (`dspark_n_routed_experts` / `dspark_num_experts_per_tok`) and one FP4 group per ug task. `MoeBuild` already took these; `MonoBuild` now carries `experts`, `topk`, `ug_groups` and `swa_width` into the MoE stage and the scratch layout.
- **SWA rows:** the draft's metadata is non-causal, with rows `get_dspark_swa_index_width(window, num_speculative_tokens)` wide (192 for window 128 and 5 drafts). K1's key-table stage read the row width as the constant 128; it reads it from the build now.
- **First layer:** the draft hands it the embedding already repeated to the hc copies, `[rows, hc, dim]`; K1 takes it as the settled residual (`fold=False`), as for the target's layer 0.
- **Its own runner:** the scratch layout depends on the number of experts, and a mailbox word must never be a tag to one launch and data to another, so the draft's layers share a second `DSV41MonoLayer` (epoch, scratch, peer buffers) as in ATOM. Every rank creates it at the same layer of the same eager step, like the target's.

Target builds are unchanged: every new field defaults to the target's value, the kernel symbols gain no suffix for them, and the ISA diff above is empty.

Limitations: MI355X (CDNA4), TP2 / TP4, steps of at most 48 rows (the draft's are 5 per request, so up to 8 requests); the layer comparison is on eager steps only. The draft's remaining per-step cost is outside its layers: `_prepare_dflash_inputs` (3 launches of 113 us), the six skinny head GEMMs (279 us), and about 75 small elementwise and copy kernels. I found no open PR doing this. Developed and measured with Claude Code; the submitter's line-by-line review is still pending.

---

commits.pr_title: [ROCm][Bugfix] Release vLLM's communicators on external-launcher shutdown
commits.pr_body:
Motivation: https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/95633/list?jid=01a14c8b-4acc-4866-b9b8-e31d71cdc245&tab=output

`ExecutorWithExternalLauncher` (torchrun, `distributed_executor_backend="external_launcher"`) now destroys vLLM's model-parallel groups on shutdown, like `MultiprocExecutor`'s workers do. Without it, `:amd: (MI355) Distributed DP + EP` intermittently aborts at exit on the ROCm 10 image (#58761).

- Fixes the exit-time abort (`terminate called without an active exception`, SIGABRT on several ranks) of `examples/features/torchrun/torchrun_dp_example_offline.py --tp-size=2 --dp-size=4 --enable-ep` on MI355 with ROCm 10.
- Only vLLM-owned groups are destroyed; the world group and the default process group, which the launcher may own, are untouched.

Root cause: `UniProcExecutor.shutdown()` only calls `worker.shutdown()`. `MultiprocExecutor` additionally calls `destroy_model_parallel()` and `destroy_distributed_environment()`, which abort the PyNCCL communicators and destroy the NCCL subgroups. In external-launcher mode nothing does, so each rank exits with live RCCL communicators whose background threads are destroyed by static destructors; a `std::thread` destroyed while joinable calls `std::terminate`. ROCm 7.2's RCCL tolerates this; ROCm 10's does not, intermittently.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Attention] Fix Triton MLA decode int32 overflow and logits workspace accounting
commits.pr_body:
Triton MLA models crash at their default context length on MI355: `vllm serve` with default settings for Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct, LongCat-Flash-Lite-FP8 and DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat dies with `Memory access fault by GPU ... Write access to a read-only page` during CUDA graph capture. Two bugs are involved, and the second only shows up once the first is fixed:

1. **int32 overflow in the decode kernels.** The split-KV logits offset `cur_batch * stride_mid_ob` is computed in int32. At ≥ 128K context, `_compute_num_kv_splits` picks 512 splits on MI355 (2 × 256 CUs), so with 32 heads one request's logits span 32 × 512 × 513 = 8.4M floats. From batch row 256 onward the offset passes 2^31, and FULL graph capture runs batches up to 512.
2. **The logits workspace is not counted by memory profiling.** #46819 reserves the worst-case logits workspace (32 GiB for LongCat at defaults: 1024 seqs × 32 heads × 512 splits × 513 × fp32) when the metadata builder is created, which happens after profiling. The KV cache is then sized as if that memory were free, and its allocation OOMs (`Tried to allocate 164.67 GiB`, 157.84 GiB free).

To resolve the above, this PR modifies:
- `triton_decode_attention.py`: compute `cur_batch * stride_mid_ob` in int64 at the six logits offsets (stage 1 normal/grouped stores and stage 2 loads), following #47671.
- `MLAAttentionImpl.reserve_profiling_workspace()`: a no-op hook called from the MLA profiling branch, next to the existing `kv_b_proj` scratch simulation.
- `TritonMLAImpl` overrides the hook to reserve the logits workspace at its upper bound (`max_num_seqs × max_decode_query_len`) during profiling. The builder keeps its reservation, which becomes a no-op.
- `test_triton_decode_attention.py`: a regression test whose logits exceed 2^31 elements, for the grouped (MLA) and normal kernels.

## Validation

MI355, TP1. `main` vs this PR:

| | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct, default 1M context | memory access fault | serves, GSM8K 87.34 |
| LongCat-Flash-Lite-FP8, default 320K context | memory access fault | serves, GSM8K 86.88 |
| DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat, default backend (`TRITON_MLA`) and 160K context | memory access fault | serves |
| LongCat with only the overflow fix | — | OOM at KV cache allocation |
| LongCat with only the accounting fix | — | memory access fault |

Both models were also served at concurrency 384, where decode rows ≥ 256 run with 512 splits: 0 failed requests.

At 32K context, where `main` works (decode TPOT Δ, + is faster; median of 5 reps, repeated with GPUs swapped):

| Model | C1 | C8 | C32 | C128 | GSM8K main → PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B-Instruct | +0.4 / +0.3% | +0.2 / +0.3% | −0.1 / +2.1% | +2.2 / +2.1% | 86.88 → 86.58 (McNemar p = 0.75) |
| LongCat-Flash-Lite-FP8 | +1.0 / +0.6% | +1.7 / +1.6% | +3.6 / +3.0% | +6.0 / +5.3% | 86.88 → 87.34 (p = 0.57) |

<details>
<summary>Why decode got faster</summary>

A rocprofv3 trace of the same LongCat decode workload (128 × 2048-token prompts, 256 output tokens, 32K context) shows all of the difference in `_fwd_grouped_kernel_stage1`: 6062 → 5230 ms (−13.7%), with identical grids and register counts. Every other kernel is within ±0.5%. In the stage-1 variants I inspected, the int32 offset lowers the logits stores to scalar `buffer_store_dword`, while the int64 base produces vectorized `global_store_dwordx3`. The kernel microbenchmark is neutral at long sequences (30 shapes, H 16–128, 4K–128K context: median 1.000×, range 0.990–1.005×, run-to-run drift ≤ 0.8%) and 15–17% faster at 512 splits with batch ≥ 128.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Tests</summary>

- `test_decode_attention_int64_logits_offset` faults on `main` (both cases) and passes with this PR in 2.4 s. It uses ~8.6 GB of fp32 logits.
- `tests/kernels/attention/test_triton_decode_attention.py` + `test_triton_mla_causal_verify_flatten.py`: 133 passed, 10/10 loops.
- `v1/attention/test_mla_backends.py` + `test_sparse_mla_backends.py` (the CI command): 11 clean runs (751 passed), including all 6 with `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1`. The 7 other runs failed only in tests that behave the same on `main`:
  - The sparse `ROCMAiterMLA` decode test fails about 1 in 20 in isolation: 19/20 on both `main` and this PR.
  - HF API 429 rate limits, from four loops running in parallel.
  - `test_chunked_context_backend_correctness` failed only in runs that also hit 429s. It is 20/20 in isolation on both `main` and this PR.
  - One transient engine OOM, where device-wide free memory dropped during profiling.
- `v1/attention` (rest of the CI command, CI environment): 1972 passed.
- DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat on `ROCM_AITER_MLA` (`VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1`, `VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER_MOE=0`), where the hook is a no-op, serves normally. AITER MoE was turned off only because this image's AITER `topk_gating` rejects `num_shared_experts` on `main`.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Design notes</summary>

- **Effect on KV cache size:** the KV cache now excludes the logits workspace. LongCat at 32K goes from 164.67 to 162.91 GiB (`main` over-commits there too, but its slack absorbs it). At 320K it is 134.86 GiB, where `main` cannot start.
- **Upper bound:** the profiling hook has no builder, so it sizes rows as `max_num_seqs × max_decode_query_len`. That matches the builder's `reorder_batch_threshold` except with DCP on a backend without varlen support, where the builder uses 1 and the profiled reservation is larger than needed.
- **Why the profiling forward:** the impl is built at model load, but the decode metadata builder only exists after profiling. Reserving in the profiling run follows the existing MLA `kv_b_proj` simulation and the sparse-indexer reservations, and avoids touching the worker's profiling code.
- **History:** #33529 made split counts up to 2 × compute units reachable, and #46819 moved the logits into a workspace reserved after profiling. #47671 fixed the same overflow class for page offsets in these kernels.
- **Duplicate check:** no open PR or issue covers this. #46728 (NVIDIA shared-memory OOR) and #57094 (NaN on empty `seq_len`) touch the same kernels for different bugs.

</details>

commits.pr_title: [ROCm][CI] Pin Inductor pointwise configs in the MoRIIO dummy-weight P/D test
commits.pr_body:
- Turn off Inductor pointwise autotuning (`triton.autotune_pointwise`) next to deterministic mode in `test_write_dummy_e2e_rocm.py`, and update the comment and docstring that explain why

Since the ROCm 10 image became the default (#58761), the attention-only cases fail with first-token log-prob distances of one or two bf16 steps (0.03-0.14), e.g. https://buildkite.com/vllm/ci/builds/95663. P/D is not involved: two plain direct serves of the same model on the same GPU disagree by the same amount, while each server is bitwise stable across repeats. Inductor's deterministic mode only pins reduction configs and still picks the XBLOCK of pointwise kernels by timing. On ROCm the XBLOCK changes which multiply-adds of the fused QK-norm + RoPE kernel get contracted into FMAs (e.g. 4 unfused packed adds at XBLOCK 1024, none at 4096), and the candidates are within timing noise of each other, so each server ends up with a random config. Pinning every pointwise kernel's config in two fresh processes makes them agree bitwise; flipping only the QK-norm + RoPE kernel's XBLOCK reproduces the CI distances.

With this change the CI-failing `qwen3_dense-TRITON_ATTN-P_FULL_AND_PIECEWISE-D_FULL_AND_PIECEWISE` case passes 10/10 on MI355 with ROCm 10 (distances exactly 0.0, full external prefix-cache hits).

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][KV Connector] Pair non-divisible hybrid MLA block sizes in NixlConnector
commits.pr_body:
NixlConnector now pairs P/D blocks of a hybrid MLA model when neither block size divides the other. That happens when P and D run different TP on ROCm. Kimi-K3 with P TP2 (2944-token blocks) and D TP1 (5760) used to fail the handshake and now runs.  Hybrid block sizes follow the TP-sharded SSM page, so P and D pick different sizes when their TP differs. On CUDA, MLA backends force 64-token kernel blocks, so the sizes always divide. ROCm AITER MLA accepts any kernel block size, so `block_size_ratio` asserts. During the handshake, `_split_remote_blocks` now views the remote blocks as gcd-sized kernel blocks (2944 → 23 × 128). The existing `block_size_ratio > 1` path then pairs them with D's 45 sub-blocks and zeroes the untransferred tail. This only applies to hybrid MLA with plainly strided remote regions. With prefix caching on, D still rejects such pairs through the existing hybrid check, as on CUDA.

- Hybrid MLA P/D with non-divisible block sizes transfers in gcd-sized units (128 tokens for Kimi-K3) instead of asserting at the handshake.
- Pairs that work today never reach the new code, so they are unaffected.

On MI355 with AITER MLA:
- `test_prefix_cache.py -k pd-tp2-dep2` (Kimi-K3): failed the handshake before; now 4/4 pass, 10/10 runs.
- Also added a new `test_hetero_non_divisible_block_sizes`: 28 fail before, 28 pass after.

## Overview

Under DBO, `DeepEPHTPrepareAndFinalize` has DeepEP allocate its dispatch outputs on the DBO comm stream, then reads them on the compute stream; the combine input crosses the other way. The caching allocator is never told about these cross-stream reads, so the other microbatch's next DeepEP call can reuse a block and overwrite it before it is read. With the DeepGEMM FP8 MoE this crashes the engine at startup with an illegal memory access in `ep_scatter`. This PR calls `record_stream` on every tensor that crosses between the two streams.

A GitHub search found no existing issue or PR for this. Related: #46990 added a ROCm-only host sync after HT dispatch/combine under DBO, possibly for the same hazard (see Details). #27666 and #38451 fixed other DBO + DeepEP HT problems.

## Claims

- Fixes the startup crash with DBO + DeepEP high-throughput + the DeepGEMM FP8 MoE (`VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM=1 VLLM_MOE_USE_DEEP_GEMM=1`, the defaults). For GLM-5.3 FP8 on main, 2 of 2 runs crashed in the first microbatched step without the fix. On 0.29.0, so did all 7 runs that had neither the fix nor a serializing workaround (`CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING`, no caching allocator, host sync). With the fix, full GSM8K scores 0.927 with CUTLASS linears and 0.912 with DeepGEMM linears (DBO off: 0.923).
- Covers both directions for every experts backend behind DeepEP HT: DeepEP's outputs (comm stream to compute stream) and the reduced expert output passed to combine (compute stream to comm stream; defensive on main, see Details). With `--enable-dbo`, main runs Model Runner V1 unless `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1` is set. MRV2's opt-in DBO uses the same microbatch contexts and streams, so it gets the same fix. Only Model Runner V1 was run.
- No change when DBO is off. With DBO on, there are no host syncs and no extra kernels. The cost is at most 9 `record_stream` calls per MoE layer per microbatch, plus one CUDA event per recorded block when it is freed; the allocator reuses that block only after the event completes. The throughput cost was not measured.
- DeepEP low-latency, NIXL-EP and DeepEP v2 are not affected, because on main they do not switch streams under DBO. `deepep_ll.py` is unchanged. The open #52177 adds the same comm-stream switching to DeepEP v2, so it may need the same treatment.

## Validation

**On main, without and with this PR.** Setup: GLM-5.3 FP8 on 1 x 8 H200, DP4 x TP2, EP8, `--all2all-backend deepep_high_throughput --enable-dbo`, `cudagraph_mode NONE`, fp8 KV, prefix caching, Model Runner V1. Env: `VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM=1 VLLM_MOE_USE_DEEP_GEMM=1 VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM_E8M0=0 VLLM_DEEP_GEMM_WARMUP=skip`; the logs show `Using DEEPGEMM Fp8 MoE backend`. Build: main @ 4a705c7b + #60732 + #60734. Running GLM-5.x with DBO needs both of those; this PR is independent of them. Eval: `lm_eval` GSM8K 5-shot, 1,319 questions, `num_concurrent=256`, standard error ±0.007–0.008. Microbatched steps were counted with a diagnostic log that is not part of this PR.

| Linears | DBO | This PR | GSM8K flexible / strict | Microbatched steps per worker |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CUTLASS (`--linear-backend cutlass`) | on | no | crash in the profile run, 2 / 2 runs | dies in the first one (2 x 4,096 tokens) |
| CUTLASS | on | yes | 0.927 / 0.927 | 100–149 |
| DeepGEMM | on | yes | 0.912 / 0.913 | 100–149 |
| DeepGEMM | off | yes (no-op) | 0.923 / 0.923 | 0 |

DeepGEMM-linears DBO on and DBO off differ by 0.010, about one standard error of the difference. We did not run CUTLASS linears with DBO off, or DeepGEMM linears with DBO on without the fix, on main. On 0.29.0 the latter crashes the same way (see below).

The crash without the fix:

| Run | What fails |
|---|---|
| no fix | The server never becomes ready. In the first microbatched step of the profile run, one worker raises `RuntimeError: DeepEP error: CPU recv timeout` in `buffer.dispatch`. The other microbatch thread gets `CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered` at `comm_stream.wait_event`, and the run ends with `torch.cat(): expected a non-empty list of Tensors`. |
| no fix, CUDA core dump | `CUDA Exception: Warp Out-of-range Address` in `_fwd_kernel_ep_scatter_2<<<(8192,1,1),(256,1,1)>>>` at `deep_gemm_utils.py:109`, which is `tl.load(expert_map + expert_id)` in `apply_expert_map`, inlined from `:241` (`expert_id = tl.load(recv_topk + ...)`). The faulting SASS loads `expert_map + expert_id * 4` after the `expert_id != -1` check, so the expert id read from the `torch.where` over DeepEP's topk ids was out of range. |

**Isolating the cause on vLLM 0.29.0.** Same 1-node GLM-5.3 setup, with backports of #60732 and #60734, DeepGEMM MoE and CUTLASS linears unless noted. The record_stream rows use an env-gated version of this patch: same three call sites, using `torch.cuda.current_stream()`.

| Variant | Questions | GSM8K flexible / strict | Microbatched steps per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| no fix: stock 0.29.0; with backports; with backports + the `ep_gather` int64 fix from fe284ea17 (#53914); DeepGEMM or CUTLASS linears; with a core dump | | crash in the profile run, 5 / 5 runs. Core dump: same kernel and source line as on main (`deep_gemm_utils.py:110` on 0.29) | |
| no fix, `VLLM_DBO_COMM_SMS=0` | | crash | |
| no fix, `VLLM_RANDOMIZE_DP_DUMMY_INPUTS=1` | | crash | |
| no fix, `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1` | 200 | 0.920 / 0.920 | 69 |
| no fix, `PYTORCH_NO_CUDA_MEMORY_CACHING=1` | 200 | 0.945 / 0.945 | 71 |
| no fix, host sync after HT dispatch/combine (the ROCm path forced on) | 300 | 0.943 / 0.943 | 90 |
| record_stream | 1,319 | 0.926 / 0.926 | 118 |
| record_stream, DeepGEMM linears | 1,319 | 0.923 / 0.923 | 132 |
| reference: no fix, FLASHINFER_CUTLASS MoE, DeepGEMM linears | 1,319 | 0.926 / 0.927 | 124 |
| reference: DBO off, DeepGEMM MoE and linears | 1,319 | 0.919 / 0.919 | 0 |

Taken together, these runs narrow the cause:
- Disabling the SM partition and randomizing the dummy inputs do not help.
- Serializing launches, disabling the caching allocator, a host sync, or `record_stream` alone each remove the crash.
- The FLASHINFER_CUTLASS MoE is fine with the same DeepGEMM linears.

That points at allocator reuse of DeepEP's buffers across DBO streams, which only the DeepGEMM MoE turns into a crash.

**Production shape (vLLM 0.29.0).** Setup: 4 x 8 H200, one engine per GPU (TP1, DP32/EP32, external load balancing), GLM-5.3-BF16 quantized online with `fp8_per_block`, DeepEP HT, eager, prefix caching, fp8 KV, `--max-num-batched-tokens 4096`, `--gpu-memory-utilization 0.70`. Each row is one run with the same backports as above. Prefill load: three waves of 1,536 unique prompts of about 9.7k tokens each, `max_tokens=1`, 6 in flight per rank. GSM8K (1,319 questions) was then run against rank 0.

| MoE / linears | DBO | Fix | GSM8K flexible / strict | Microbatched steps per worker | KV cache per GPU (tokens) | Prefill tok/s, wave 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FLASHINFER_CUTLASS / CUTLASS (FlashInfer autotune off*) | on | no | 0.924 / 0.923 | 278 | 645k | 79.4k |
| DeepGEMM / DeepGEMM | on | record_stream | 0.917 / 0.917 | 280 | 736k min, 796k median | 75.0k |
| DeepGEMM / DeepGEMM | off | n/a | 0.925 / 0.925 | 0 | 733k min, 803k median | 67.5k |

\* Two earlier attempts with FlashInfer autotune on stalled during startup autotuning. Throughput is the third wave over all 32 GPUs. DeepGEMM kernels JIT-compile during the first waves (`VLLM_DEEP_GEMM_WARMUP=skip`), and all three runs were still speeding up in wave 3, so these are not steady-state numbers. This table shows that DBO + DeepGEMM MoE works at production scale with the fix. It is not a performance claim for this PR. Without the fix this configuration does not start, so measuring the fix's own cost needs a MoE backend that runs either way, such as FLASHINFER_CUTLASS. We did not do that.

**CI coverage.** This PR adds no test. The existing DBO test, `tests/v1/distributed/test_dbo.py` (DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat, DP2), already runs the changed lines in its `deepep_high_throughput` case, with a BF16 MoE (`TritonExperts`) rather than the DeepGEMM path. It runs in the 2 x H100 "Distributed Features" job (optional), the B200 "Distributed" job (also optional; xfailed on Blackwell for unstable DBO accuracy; we have not checked whether that is related) and the AMD mirrors. With this patch, on 2 x H200 it passes both cases (`deepep_low_latency`, `deepep_high_throughput`) in 9 minutes, with 200+ microbatched steps per worker in the HT case. To build a 2-GPU reproducer, we quantized that model's MoE online to block FP8 with `--quantization online --quantization-config '{"moe": "fp8_per_block"}' --moe-backend deep_gemm`. The logs confirm the DEEPGEMM MoE behind `DeepEPHTPrepareAndFinalize`. That variant passed without the fix every time, so it cannot catch a regression:

| DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat (H200, threshold 0.62) | This PR | GSM8K strict | Microbatched steps per worker |
|---|---|---|---|
| DP2, 256 questions | no | 0.648 | 200+ |
| DP2, `--max-num-batched-tokens 16384 --max-num-seqs 256`, 512 questions | no | 0.666 | 200+ |
| DP8 / EP8, 256 questions | no | 0.652 | 100+ |
| DP2, 256 questions | yes | 0.645 | 200+ |

It would add DeepGEMM-MoE coverage of the patched path for 5–7 minutes on 2 GPUs. We can add it if reviewers want it, but it would not have caught this bug. The regression evidence is the manual GLM-5.3 runs above. Separately, quantizing V2-Lite's linears as well (`--quantization fp8_per_block`) scored about 0 on GSM8K in this DBO setup, both with and without this PR. That is unrelated and was not investigated.

**Lint:** pre-commit passes on the rebased commit: ruff check and format (0.14.0), typos (1.43.5), mypy (1.20.2), and the local SPDX, forbidden-import, `torch.cuda` and boolean-context-manager hooks. Before the rebase, with torch types resolved, mypy reported 2 errors, which also appear on the unpatched file.

**Not run:**
- Model Runner V2 with DBO (opt-in via `VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=1`). It uses the same code path.
- ROCm. The AMD CI mirrors run `test_dbo.py` with DeepEP HT, so CI will exercise the change there.
- `tests/kernels/moe/test_deepep*.py` with this patch. They do not enable DBO, so the change is a no-op in them.
- Multi-node on main.
- Whether this fixes the DeepSeek-V3.2 DBO illegal memory access noted in #60734 (see Details).
- The GPU runs on main used 4a705c7b. This branch is rebased on main @ 240785b8 (the rebase did not change the patch: same `git patch-id`), where `deepep_ht.py`, `ubatching.py`, `gpu_ubatch_wrapper.py` and `gpu/ubatch_utils.py` are unchanged. `deep_gemm_utils.py`, `deep_gemm_moe.py` and `modular_kernel.py` changed in between (#58373, #59128, #49194). On the rebased commit we re-ran `pytest -v -s tests/v1/distributed/test_dbo.py` on 2 x H200: 2 passed (`deepep_low_latency`, `deepep_high_throughput`) in 9 minutes. The GLM-5.3 runs were not repeated on the newer base.

<details>
<summary>Reproduction commands</summary>

```bash
# GLM-5.3 with DBO also needs #60732 and #60734.
VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM=1 VLLM_MOE_USE_DEEP_GEMM=1 VLLM_USE_DEEP_GEMM_E8M0=0 VLLM_DEEP_GEMM_WARMUP=skip \
vllm serve zai-org/GLM-5.3 --tensor-parallel-size 2 --data-parallel-size 4 --enable-expert-parallel \
  --all2all-backend deepep_high_throughput --enable-dbo --compilation-config '{"cudagraph_mode": "NONE"}' \
  --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --max-model-len 8192 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90 --enable-prefix-caching \
  --linear-backend cutlass   # omit for DeepGEMM linears
lm_eval --model local-completions \
  --model_args model=zai-org/GLM-5.3,base_url=http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/completions,num_concurrent=256,tokenized_requests=False \
  --tasks gsm8k --num_fewshot 5

# Without this PR the server fails during startup (profile run). To get the core dump, add:
CUDA_ENABLE_COREDUMP_ON_EXCEPTION=1 \
CUDA_COREDUMP_GENERATION_FLAGS=skip_nonrelocated_elf_images,skip_global_memory,skip_shared_memory,skip_local_memory \
CUDA_COREDUMP_FILE=core_%h_%p.nvcudmp
cuda-gdb -ex 'target cudacore core_<host>_<pid>.nvcudmp'
```
</details>

## Details

**Root cause** (main @ 240785b8, before this PR):
- **Shared streams.** `UBatchWrapper` creates one comm stream (`gpu_ubatch_wrapper.py:76`) and gives both microbatches that comm stream and the same compute stream (`:288-291`). MRV2's `UBatchRunner` does the same (`gpu/ubatch_utils.py:327,458-462`).
- **Where DeepEP allocates.** `_do_dispatch` switches to the comm stream (`deepep_ht.py:126`). It then calls `get_dispatch_layout` and `dispatch` with `allocate_on_comm_stream=False` (`:139,168`) and, under DBO, `async_finish=False` (`:138,167`). DeepEP therefore allocates recv x, scales, topk ids and topk weights on the current stream, which is the DBO comm stream's allocator pool. It runs its kernels on its own internal stream, which waits only on `previous_event`. With `async_finish=False` it then makes the calling stream wait for that internal stream, and it records no other stream on its tensors: its HT dispatch and combine call `record_stream` only when `async_finish=True` (`csrc/deep_ep.cpp`).
- **Where they are read and freed.** `dbo_switch_to_compute_sync()` (`:177`) orders the compute stream after the dispatch, and `_receiver` reads the outputs there: first the `torch.where` over the topk ids (`:225`), then the experts. Once those kernels are enqueued the Python references are dropped; for example, `expert_topk_ids` is rebound by the `torch.where`. The blocks go back to the comm pool, free for any later comm-stream work.
- **How they get overwritten.** The other microbatch's next DeepEP call allocates from the same comm-stream pool. Its kernels wait only on its own `previous_event`, captured on the compute stream before it yielded (#38451). The DBO comm stream itself waits only on that microbatch's compute-done event (`ubatching.py:86-87`, recorded in `yield_and_switch_from_compute_to_comm` before the yield). Both events were recorded before this microbatch enqueued its reads. So that call's outputs can land in the freed blocks and be written before the reads run. The DeepGEMM contiguous path then loads `expert_map[expert_id]` for whatever id it finds (`deep_gemm_utils.py:107-110`, called from `_fwd_kernel_ep_scatter_2` at `:244-247`), which is the faulting load in the core dump.
- **Reverse direction.** For experts that leave the weight-and-reduce to the prepare/finalize (`TopKWeightAndReduceDelegate`), `_finalize` reduces into a new compute-stream tensor (`apply(output=None)`, `:365`), and combine reads it on the comm stream (`:376`). `dbo_switch_to_compute()` (`:389`) does not order the compute stream after the combine. The tensor is freed when `_finalize` returns, so later compute-stream work, such as shared experts or the other microbatch, can reuse the block while combine is still reading it. On main, though, no experts class that can run behind DeepEP HT delegates: the delegating classes all use the batched activation format, DeepEP HT uses the standard one, and the standard CUTLASS FP8 and Marlin experts return `TopKWeightAndReduceNoOP`. Every experts class that can run behind DeepEP HT reduces itself (DeepGEMM, Triton, FlashInfer CUTLASS, ...), so the combine input is the per-microbatch workspace (or the caller's output tensor when the shapes match), which is not freed there. The `_finalize` call (1 of the 9) is therefore defensive on main, for a future delegating experts class. We did not observe this direction.
- **Dispatch inputs.** Tokens, scales, topk ids and topk weights are already safe today, because they are freed only after `dbo_switch_to_compute_sync()` makes the compute stream wait on the comm stream. They are recorded anyway (4 of the 9 calls), so their safety does not depend on that ordering; this is also the version validated on 0.29.

**Fix:** `_dbo_record_stream()` calls `t.record_stream(current_stream())` on each non-`None` tensor when `dbo_enabled()`. It is called in three places:
- in `_do_dispatch`, after switching to comm, on the dispatch inputs (compute to comm);
- in `_receiver`, before the `torch.where`, on DeepEP's outputs (comm to compute);
- in `_finalize`, after switching to comm, on the reduced expert output (compute to comm).

When a recorded tensor is freed, the allocator records an event on the consuming stream and does not reuse the block until that event has completed. For the two compute-to-comm sites the actual reader is DeepEP's internal stream. Recording the DBO comm stream still covers it, because with `async_finish=False` the DBO comm stream waits for DeepEP's kernels before dispatch or combine returns, and the tensors are freed after that. DeepEP's handle and layout tensors and `combined_x` are used only on the DBO comm stream and DeepEP's internal stream, so they are not recorded (but see "Not covered").

CUDA graphs: DeepEP HT is never captured. vLLM forces `cudagraph_mode` NONE for HT with DP > 1, and DBO needs DP > 1. PyTorch also supports `record_stream` during capture.

**Why FLASHINFER_CUTLASS does not crash, but may still race.** The hazard is in the prepare/finalize, so it does not depend on the experts backend; what differs is what a corrupted id does. FlashInfer's CUTLASS MoE receives `ep_rank`/`ep_size` and keeps only ids in this rank's range (`expert >= start_expert && expert < end_expert`, `cutlass_fused_moe_kernels.cuh:223,449` in FlashInfer 0.7.0.post1). A garbage id is therefore dropped instead of dereferenced, and garbage activations or weights would only produce wrong numbers. With FLASHINFER_CUTLASS, DBO matches DBO off on GSM8K: 0.922–0.927 on main in #60734, and 0.924 at EP32 above. So we have no evidence that the race fires there in practice. We also do not know why the window opens reliably for GLM-5.3 with DeepGEMM but not for DeepSeek-V2-Lite with DeepGEMM. #60734 notes an illegal memory access with DeepSeek-V3.2 and DBO that also uses FLASHINFER_CUTLASS and also disappears with `CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1`. We have not tested whether this PR fixes it.

**Why ROCm already host-syncs.** #46990 added `_sync_dbo_comm_if_needed` (`deepep_ht.py:61,71-76`), a host `synchronize()` of the current stream after HT dispatch and combine under DBO, on ROCm only. Its comment cites reuse of "Buffer-owned communication workspace". Forcing the same sync on CUDA also removed the crash (0.29 table). We suspect ROCm hit the same allocator hazard, but we have no ROCm hardware to check, so this PR leaves the ROCm sync in place; on ROCm, `record_stream` only adds bookkeeping.

<details>
<summary>Alternatives considered</summary>

1. Use the host sync on CUDA as well. It works (0.29 table), but it blocks the CPU after every HT dispatch and combine of every microbatch: 300 times per step for GLM-5.3's 75 MoE layers. That gives up the CPU run-ahead DBO needs for overlap. Not benchmarked.
2. `allocate_on_comm_stream=True`. This moves the outputs to DeepEP's internal stream, but the compute stream still reads them, so on its own it does not order reuse. DeepEP also accepts it only together with `previous_event` and `async_finish=True`, and vLLM disables `async_finish` under DBO. Not tried.
3. `record_stream` (this PR). It marks exactly the tensors that cross streams, adds no syncs or kernels, and keeps the fix inside the one prepare/finalize that switches streams under DBO.
</details>

**Not covered:** blocks freed on the comm stream itself, for example `combined_x` after `output.copy_` in the finalize receiver, are reused by later comm-stream allocations. DeepEP's kernels for that later call wait on `previous_event`, a compute-stream event, rather than on the comm stream, so in principle they could run before the earlier comm-stream copy finishes. We inferred this from DeepEP's source (its internal stream waits on `previous_event` when one is given, otherwise on the calling stream) and have not observed it. `record_stream` cannot express this ordering. Passing `previous_event=None` under DBO would make DeepEP wait on the comm stream instead. That is left for a follow-up because it changes the ordering #38451 tuned.

**Related:**
- #60732 fixes the DSA indexer crash under DBO.
- #60734 fixes DSA shared top-k under DBO.
- #60733 clamps `BLOCK_SIZE_K` in the batched Triton FP8 MoE.
- #52177 (open) adds DBO to DeepEP v2 with the same comm-stream switching as HT.

The first three came out of the same GLM-5.3 bring-up and are independent of this PR. The `ep_gather` int64 fix in fe284ea17 (#53914) is already on main; the 0.29 no-fix runs crash with and without a backport of it.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Rust Frontend] Use xgrammar for gRPC structured outputs
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

The Rust frontend's gRPC server lowers every structured-output constraint to the guidance backend (#44729). Guidance only parses the legacy `triggers`/`structures` structural tag (#55152), so gRPC clients that send xgrammar-format structural tags for tool calling get `INTERNAL` on every request. This PR makes the gRPC path use xgrammar for every constraint, as Python's `auto` does, teaches the xgrammar backend to compile `choice` itself, and applies Python's xgrammar schema check in the Rust frontend's shared request validation.

## Claims

- gRPC `structural_tag` constraints in the current `{"type": "structural_tag", "format": ...}` shape compile and constrain output instead of failing in EngineCore with `KeyError: 'triggers'`.
- All gRPC structured-output requests select one backend, so a gRPC-served engine no longer depends on which request arrives first to pick its backend.
- The xgrammar backend compiles `choice` requests with the same EBNF grammar Python's `choice_as_grammar` produces, so frontends that skip Python request validation can send `choice` as is. This also fixes Rust HTTP `choice` requests failing with `grammar is not of valid supported types` once xgrammar is the engine's backend.
- JSON schemas that use keywords xgrammar ignores are rejected when the request's backend is xgrammar, with Python's message, instead of being silently under-enforced. gRPC returns `INVALID_ARGUMENT`; Rust HTTP would return 400, though no HTTP constraint takes this path yet.
- Regexes containing NUL are rejected in `StructuredOutputsParams::validate`, as Python does for every backend. This also applies to the Rust HTTP routes.

## Validation

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on GB200 through the Dynamo vLLM sidecar, which talks to `vllm-rs` over gRPC and sends xgrammar-format structural tags for tool calls (ai-dynamo/dynamo#16494). Same vLLM nightly in both columns; the right column adds an earlier revision of this commit (xgrammar for every gRPC constraint plus the `choice` rewrite) to `vllm-rs`.

| Check | vLLM main | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| `tool_choice: auto` + one tool | HTTP 500 (gRPC `INTERNAL`, `KeyError: 'triggers'`) | HTTP 200 |
| Dynamo tool-calling suite (48 cases) | not run, every tool request 500s | 47/48 (the miss is tool markup inside reasoning, also intermittent on other runtimes) |
| BFCL sample (50 cases) | not run | 39/50, all HTTP 200 (other Dynamo runtimes score 38 to 43 on this model) |

Tests on the current head:

- Rust: `cargo nextest run -p vllm-engine-core-client -p vllm-text -p vllm-server`: 713 passed. `unary_generate_invalid_structured_outputs_returns_invalid_argument` sends an empty grammar, an empty choice, a NUL regex and an xgrammar-unsupported schema through the real gRPC server against the mock engine and expects `INVALID_ARGUMENT` for each. With the text-lowering validation removed, the request reaches the engine and the test fails.
- Python: `test_xgrammar_compiles_choice_without_rewrite` compiles an unrewritten `choice` request through `get_structured_output_key`. It fails without the backend change (`grammar is not of valid supported types. (StructuredOutputOptions.CHOICE)`) and passes with it. `test_backend_xgrammar.py` and `test_backend_xgrammar_lark.py` have the same results with and without this PR.

## Details

**Root cause.** `StructuredOutputManager` creates one backend from the first structured-output request it sees and compiles every later request with it (`vllm/v1/structured_output/__init__.py`). The Rust frontend skips Python's `SamplingParams` validation, which is where `_backend` is normally chosen, so #44729 set the backend to guidance, which handles `choice` natively. The guidance backend reads structural tags in the legacy shape only. The `format` shape that tool-calling clients and the Rust chat path (#46057) produce raises `KeyError: 'triggers'` in `GuidanceBackend.compile_grammar`, the request finishes with an error, and the gRPC server returns `INTERNAL`.

**Why every constraint, not only structural tags.** With xgrammar for structural tags and guidance for the rest, whichever kind of request reached the engine first would decide the backend, and the other kind would fail. One backend for the whole gRPC path avoids that.

**Where the xgrammar checks live.** Python's `validate_xgrammar_grammar` rewrites `choice` into a grammar (the xgrammar backend has no `choice` path), and `auto` keeps schemas that `has_xgrammar_unsupported_json_features` flags away from xgrammar. The Rust frontend bypasses that validation. Both rules depend on the backend, not on the protocol, so neither goes into the gRPC converter:

- `choice`: `XgrammarBackend.compile_grammar` compiles `CHOICE` with `choice_as_grammar`, as #58321 did for Lark. Every frontend sends `choice` unchanged, and the grammar has one implementation.
- Unsupported schema keywords: `has_unsupported_json_features` is ported into `engine-core-client`, and `StructuredOutputsParams::validate` rejects such schemas when the backend is xgrammar. Text lowering (`lower_sampling_params`) validates the final constraint for every route, after chat may have replaced the user's constraint with a parser-built output grammar. The error maps to 400 / `INVALID_ARGUMENT`. The gRPC converter only selects xgrammar and no longer validates on its own.

Python's NUL-in-regex rejection is backend-independent, so it goes into `StructuredOutputsParams::validate` next to the other early checks.

**Tradeoff.** Python's `auto` sends schemas with keywords xgrammar ignores (`multipleOf`, `uniqueItems`/`contains`, unsupported string `format`s, `pattern` with length bounds, some `propertyNames`/`patternProperties` combinations, multi-branch `allOf`) to guidance. EngineCore holds one backend, so the gRPC path cannot do that per request. It now rejects them with `INVALID_ARGUMENT`, as Python does when the backend is `xgrammar`, rather than accepting them and enforcing less than the schema says. gRPC clients that relied on guidance for those keywords will see the error.

**Not changed.** Python also parses grammars, regexes and schemas with xgrammar up front; on the gRPC path an invalid constraint still fails at EngineCore compile time, as it did under guidance. The Rust frontend has no JSON nesting cap (#60036) on any route, before or after this PR. Python's `auto` sends Lark grammars for Tekken Mistral tokenizers to guidance; on the gRPC path they now use xgrammar.

**Not a duplicate.**
- #55258 (closed) moved all Rust-frontend structured outputs to xgrammar and added a `choice` path to the Python xgrammar backend. Its author noted that the engine supporting several backends at once may be the right long-term direction. This PR is narrower: it changes the gRPC backend choice, adds the same `choice` path to the Python xgrammar backend, and adds the backend-keyed schema check and the NUL check to shared Rust validation, with no CLI changes. It fixes a hard failure now and does not get in the way of engine-side multi-backend support.
- #55153 (open) teaches the guidance backend some `format` shapes (`triggered_tags`, `tags_with_separator`, `any_text`) and rejects the rest. xgrammar compiles the full structural-tag format, and the Rust chat path already sends these tags with `backend = xgrammar` (#46057), so the gRPC path now matches it. The two PRs do not conflict.
- #49625 (open) rejects mismatched backends at validation time. It addresses the same single-backend limit from the engine side.

**Limitation / follow-up.** The Rust HTTP routes still lower native constraints to guidance while parser-built output grammars use xgrammar (#46057, #60781). A server that takes both kinds of traffic over HTTP is still order-dependent. With the xgrammar `choice` path, HTTP `choice` no longer fails when xgrammar is chosen first, but parser-built structural tags still fail when guidance is chosen first. This PR leaves those routes' backend choice unchanged; the follow-up is a single operator-selected backend for every Rust route, defaulting to xgrammar.

## Purpose

Make the GPU's per-request logit counts decide which grammar mask rows are applied, instead of a CPU-built mask→logit mapping.

- The scheduler emits a fixed-width block of `num_spec_tokens + 1` mask rows per structured-output request.
- The MRV2 kernel launches once per grammar request and applies only the positions active in device `cu_num_logits` (e.g. bonus-only after an adaptive-verification zero-budget step).
- This removes `_build_grammar_mapping` and the worker's dependence on `cu_num_logits_np` / scheduled draft counts. Batch-sharded sampling slices whole blocks, and MRV1 unpacks blocks into its packed layout.

commits.pr_title: [Bugfix][Frontend] Stop beam search on generation config EOS tokens
commits.pr_body:
## Overview

Beam search (`LLM.beam_search` and `use_beam_search` in the OpenAI server) only treats `tokenizer.eos_token_id` as the end of a beam. Normal generation also stops on the extra `eos_token_id` entries from the model's generation config. For chat models whose end-of-turn token is one of those extra ids, beam search keeps going after the answer and writes the next turn until `max_tokens`.

## Claims

- Beams finish on every EOS id that normal generation stops on (the tokenizer EOS plus the generation config's `eos_token_id`), unless `ignore_eos=True`.
- The OpenAI server reports the token that actually ended the beam as `stop_reason` and leaves it out of the text, as it already does for the tokenizer EOS. The length-normalized beam score discounts it the same way.

## Validation

[`zai-org/glm-edge-1.5b-chat`](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/glm-edge-1.5b-chat) has `<|endoftext|>` (59246) as tokenizer EOS, and its generation config adds `<|user|>` (59253) and `<|observation|>` (59255). The model ends its turn with `<|user|>`.

```python
from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams
from vllm.sampling_params import BeamSearchParams

llm = LLM("zai-org/glm-edge-1.5b-chat", enforce_eager=True, max_model_len=512)
tokenizer = llm.get_tokenizer()
text = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of France?"}],
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=False,
)
prompt = {"prompt_token_ids": tokenizer.encode(text, add_special_tokens=False)}

print(llm.generate(prompt, SamplingParams(temperature=0, max_tokens=48))[0].outputs[0].text)
beam = llm.beam_search([prompt], BeamSearchParams(beam_width=2, max_tokens=48))[0].sequences[0]
print(tokenizer.decode(beam.tokens[len(prompt["prompt_token_ids"]):], skip_special_tokens=True))
```

I ran this on an L4 with the published wheel for cffc0cfa3 (`main`) and with the same wheel plus this change. I also sent the same question to `/v1/chat/completions` with `"use_beam_search": true, "n": 2, "max_tokens": 48`:

| | `main` | This PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Greedy `LLM.generate` | `The capital of France is Paris.` (8 tokens) | same |
| `LLM.beam_search` | `The capital of France is Paris.\nThank you for the quick response! Is there another capital city …` (48 tokens, the model writing the next user turn) | `The capital of France is Paris.` (8 tokens) |
| `/v1/chat/completions` with beam search | the same kind of 48-token text, `finish_reason: length`, `stop_reason: null` | `The capital of France is Paris.`, `finish_reason: stop`, `stop_reason: 59253` |

For "Name the three primary colors.", beam search on `main` also ran to the 48-token limit. With this change it returned `The three primary colors are:\n\n1. Red\n2. Blue\n3. Yellow` with `stop_reason: 59253`.

On `microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct` (tokenizer EOS 32000, generation config `[32000, 32001, 32007]`), every beam on `main` ended in `<|end|><|endoftext|>` with `stop_reason: 32000`. With this change, beams end at `<|end|>` with `stop_reason: 32007`. Greedy generation and `ignore_eos=True` gave the same tokens before and after.

```bash
pytest tests/samplers/test_beam_search_online.py tests/samplers/test_beam_search.py -k "not test_beam_search_single_input and not test_beam_search_with_concurrency_limit and not test_beam_search_passes_multimodal_data and not test_beam_search_structured_output"
```

- The new `test_beam_search_respects_generation_config_eos` runs the offline and online beam loops with no, a scalar, or a list config EOS, with and without `ignore_eos`. 4 of its 12 cases fail on `main`.
- With this change: 37 passed. The 4 deselected tests need a GPU.
- `pre-commit run --files` on the changed files passes.

## Details

Both loops compared each candidate token with `tokenizer.eos_token_id`. The one-token engine requests they send already get the generation config applied, but the loops expand the returned logprobs and decide completion themselves.

I resolve the EOS ids once, with the existing `SamplingParams.update_from_generation_config(...)` on the beam's base sampling params. Then I use `all_stop_token_ids` in the completion check, for the online `stop_reason` and text trimming, and in `get_beam_search_score`.

Duplicate check: I searched open and closed issues and PRs for beam search with EOS, `eos_token_id`, `generation_config`, `ignore_eos` and the changed files. #9627 (merged) fixed stripping the tokenizer EOS from beam text. #52621 (beam search stop strings) and #36285 (online structured output) touch the same files but still compare with `tokenizer.eos_token_id` only. The other open PRs on these files (#60327, #60550, #59506, #47630, #60787, #55437, #60562, #51891, #60094, #52249) change unrelated parts.
